seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 272 HTS Chapter 04 lines — milk, cream, milk powder, yogurt, whey, butter, cheese, eggs, honey and edible insects. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, the dairy tariff-rate quotas, the 2026 Section 301 duties and the Canada Section 338 dairy duties.

overview.intro:
Chapter 04 covers dairy — milk, cream, milk powder, yogurt, whey, butter and cheese — plus birds' eggs, natural honey and other edible animal products such as edible insects. Its **272 tariff lines** are built around **dairy tariff-rate quotas**: most dairy products have an in-quota line (low rate, usually needing a USDA import license) and an "Other" line with a much higher over-quota rate — for cheese **$1.055 to $2.269 per kg**, for butter **$1.541/kg**. Eggs (2.8¢/dozen) and honey (1.9¢/kg) have small, single rates.

The U.S. imported **$4.06B** of Chapter 04 goods in 2025: cheese $1.70B, honey $691M, butter $494M, whey and milk proteins $447M and eggs $221M. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from the 60 Section 301 economies pay an extra duty — **10% in total for EU goods**, +12.5% for New Zealand, +10% for India, Argentina and the UK, +37.5% for Brazil. **Canada is hit hardest**: 60 lines — milk powders, whey, many cheeses and honey — pay an extra 50% under Section 338 even with a USMCA claim, and Canadian whey is banned from **September 29, 2026**. Raw honey from Argentina, Brazil, India, Vietnam and China also carries antidumping duties.

productGroups.label: Milk and cream, not concentrated or sweetened
productGroups.blurb: Fluid milk and cream. Skim and low-fat milk pay a fraction of a cent per liter; milk and cream over 6% fat are under quota (additional U.S. notes 5 and 6) at 3.2¢/liter or 12.3¢/kg in quota, 77.2¢/liter or $1.646/kg above it. Fluid milk and cream also need an FDA import milk permit.

productGroups.label: Milk and cream, concentrated or sweetened (milk powder, condensed and evaporated milk)
productGroups.blurb: Skim and whole milk powder, evaporated and condensed milk. In quota (notes 7–11; most need a USDA license) 2.2¢ to 13.7¢/kg or 17.5%; over quota 31.3¢/kg to $1.556/kg — whole milk powder pays $1.092/kg. Mexico ($102M) and Chile ($62M) are the largest suppliers. Canadian product pays an extra 50% (Section 338).

productGroups.label: Yogurt, buttermilk, sour cream, kefir and other fermented milk
productGroups.blurb: Yogurt pays 17% (dry yogurt 20% in quota, $1.035/kg + 17% over quota); sour cream, buttermilk and dried fermented milk follow the milk and cream quotas. Canada ($77M) and France ($60M) supply most of it.

productGroups.label: Whey and products of natural milk constituents (incl. whey protein and milk protein concentrates)
productGroups.blurb: Whey, whey protein concentrate (8.5%) and milk protein concentrate (0.37¢/kg) — New Zealand ($310M) is by far the largest supplier. Dried whey is under quota: 3.3¢/kg or 13% in quota, 87.6¢/kg or $1.035/kg + 8.5% over quota. **Canadian whey (0404.10) cannot be imported from September 29, 2026.**

productGroups.label: Butter, butter oil, ghee and dairy spreads
productGroups.blurb: Butter is a small quota (6,977 t a year, additional U.S. note 6): 12.3¢/kg in quota, **$1.541/kg** above it. Butter oil and anhydrous milk fat pay 10% in quota or $1.865/kg + 8.5% over quota. Ireland ($209M) and New Zealand ($167M) lead; ghee from India uses the same lines.

productGroups.label: Cheese and curd
productGroups.blurb: The biggest group: 156 lines and $1.70B of imports in 2025, led by Italy, France, Spain and the Netherlands. Most cheeses split into an in-quota line (usually 10%–25%, USDA license) and an over-quota line at $1.055–$2.269/kg; cheeses outside the quotas need no license — sheep's-milk Pecorino in original loaves (Free), other sheep's-milk cheese (9.6%), Roquefort (2.7%–4.5%), and soft-ripened Brie-type cheese or cheese without cow's milk. EU cheese pays at least 10% in total since July 24, 2026.

productGroups.label: Birds' eggs, in shell
productGroups.blurb: Table eggs, hatching eggs and preserved eggs all pay 2.8¢ per dozen. Imports jumped from $92M in 2024 to $221M in 2025 as U.S. egg supplies fell after avian influenza; Brazil, Canada, Mexico, Türkiye and the UK supplied most. Imports need USDA approval (APHIS bird-flu rules; AMS shell-egg rules).

productGroups.label: Eggs not in shell and egg yolks (liquid, frozen, dried)
productGroups.blurb: Egg products: dried whole egg or yolk 47.6¢/kg, liquid and frozen 9.7¢/kg. They are regulated by USDA FSIS under the Egg Products Inspection Act, so the exporting country must be eligible with FSIS.

productGroups.label: Natural honey
productGroups.blurb: Honey pays 1.9¢/kg, split for statistics into organic, comb or retail-packed and four color grades. The tariff is tiny; what matters is the **antidumping duties on raw honey** from Argentina, Brazil, India and Vietnam (2022 orders) and on honey from China (since 2001), plus the Section 301 duty for the country. Canadian honey pays an extra 50%.

productGroups.label: Insects and other edible animal products n.e.s. (edible bird's nests, royal jelly)
productGroups.blurb: Edible insects and insect flour (0410.10) and other edible animal products such as edible bird's nests and royal jelly (0410.90), both at 1.1%. Indonesia is the largest supplier. Insects are on the Section 301 exception lists of six countries.

workedExamples.title: A pallet of Parmigiano Reggiano from Italy
workedExamples.body: 10,000 kg at $14/kg ($140,000). Parmesan is under the Italian-type cheese quota (additional U.S. note 21). An importer holding a USDA license enters it under 0406.90.41 at **15%: $21,000**. Without a license it goes under 0406.90.42 at $2.146/kg: **$21,460**. Both are already above 10% of value, so the EU's Section 301 rule (10% in total when the base rate is lower, 9903.05.39) adds nothing.

workedExamples.title: Irish butter, in quota and over quota
workedExamples.body: 20,000 kg at $7/kg ($140,000). The butter quota is only 6,977 t a year for all countries and needs a USDA license, so most imported butter enters "Other" at **$1.541/kg: $30,820** (22% of value). Inside the quota (0405.10.10, 12.3¢/kg = $2,460) the EU rule lifts the total to **10%: $14,000**.

workedExamples.title: Aged cheddar from Canada with a USMCA claim
workedExamples.body: $100,000 of Canadian cheddar entered in quota. With a USMCA claim the base rate is Free and the 10% Section 301 duty is lifted (9903.05.93), but since **September 15, 2026** this cheese is on the Section 338 list (9903.03.12), which applies even to USMCA goods (U.S. note 51(a)): **$50,000**. Over Canada's quota it would pay $1.227/kg plus 60% (the 10% Section 301 duty returns because the entry is no longer free under USMCA).

workedExamples.title: A container of raw honey from India
workedExamples.body: 20,000 kg of light-amber raw honey in drums at $3/kg ($60,000). Base duty 1.9¢/kg: **$380**. India's Section 301 duty adds 10% (9903.05.44): **$6,000**. Raw honey from India is also under an antidumping order, so CBP collects a cash deposit at the exporter's current rate (the 2022 "all others" rate was 5.87%; Commerce resets rates in annual reviews).

workedExamples.title: Manuka honey from New Zealand, retail jars
workedExamples.body: 2,000 kg at $60/kg ($120,000). Base duty 1.9¢/kg: **$38**. New Zealand pays the 12.5% Section 301 duty (9903.05.57): **$15,000** — 99.7% of the bill. Honey packed for retail sale is outside the 2022 raw-honey antidumping orders, and New Zealand is not one of the countries they cover.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** "Milk" means full cream milk or partially or completely skimmed milk.

**Note 2.** Yogurt (heading 0403) may be concentrated or flavored and contain sugar, fruit, nuts, cocoa, spices, cereals and similar, as long as they do not replace any milk constituent and the product keeps the character of yogurt.

**Note 3.** "Butter" (heading 0405) has 80%–95% milkfat, at most 2% milk solids-not-fat and at most 16% water; "dairy spreads" are water-in-oil emulsions with 39% to under 80% milkfat as the only fat. Dehydrated butter and ghee go to 0405.90.

**Note 4.** Concentrated whey with added milk or milkfat is cheese (0406) if it has at least 5% milkfat in the dry matter, 70%–85% dry matter and can be molded.

**Note 5.** Not covered: insects unfit for human consumption (0511); whey products over 95% lactose (1702); milk products in which a natural constituent is replaced, such as filled milk (1901 or 2106); albumins, including whey protein isolates over 80% whey protein (3502), and globulins (3504).

**Note 6.** "Insects" (0410) means edible non-living insects, whole or in parts, fresh, chilled, frozen, dried, smoked, salted or in brine, and insect flours and meals; otherwise prepared insects go to section IV.

**Subheading notes.** "Modified whey" (0404.10) is whey with lactose, proteins or minerals removed or added, and mixtures of whey constituents. "Butter" in 0405.10 excludes dehydrated butter and ghee (0405.90).
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**Note 1.** "Dairy products described in additional U.S. note 1 to chapter 4" means malted milk and articles of milk or cream (except white chocolate and infrared-calibration milk powders), articles over 5.5% butterfat suitable as ingredients, and dried milk, whey or buttermilk mixtures over 16% milk solids not packed for the retail consumer.

**Note 2.** "EU 27" lists the 27 EU member states, for the cheese quota allocations.

**Note 3.** "Soft ripened cow's milk cheese" (Brie-type) has a surface-ripened crust, ripens from the surface inward, at least 50% fat in dry matter and at least 65% moisture in the non-fat matter; blue-veined cheese is excluded.

**Note 4.** Defines "capable of being further processed", "prepared for marketing to the ultimate consumer" and "ultimate consumer" (which excludes restaurants, hotels, bakeries, hospitals and similar institutions).

**Notes 5–12 and 14 — yearly quotas** (Mexico excluded from all of them): milk and cream 6%–45% fat 6,694,840 liters (New Zealand at least 5,678,117 liters); butter and cream over 45% fat 6,977,000 kg; nonfat dry milk 5,261,000 kg; dried whole milk 3,321,300 kg; dried cream 99,500 kg; note 1 dairy products 4,105,000 kg (Australia at least 1,016,046 kg); condensed and evaporated milk 6,857,300 kg; dried buttermilk and whey 296,000 kg; butter substitutes and butter oil 6,080,500 kg. Most require a USDA import license.

**Note 13.** "Milk protein concentrate" (0404.90.10) is any complete milk protein concentrate with 40% or more protein.

**Note 15.** No weight allowance for inedible protective coverings of cheese.

**Notes 16–25 — cheese quotas by type and country**, mostly needing a USDA license: other cheese (note 16: EU 27 25,632,850 kg, New Zealand 11,322,000 kg, Australia 3,050,000 kg, UK 2,213,374 kg, Switzerland 1,720,000 kg, Canada 1,141,000 kg and others); blue-mold (note 17); Cheddar (note 18: New Zealand 8,200,000 kg, Australia 2,450,000 kg, Canada 833,417 kg — Canadian aged raw-milk cheddar needs no license); American-type (19); Edam and Gouda (20); Italian-type (21: Argentina 6,383,000 kg, EU 27 5,407,000 kg); Swiss/Emmentaler without eyes and Gruyère-process (22); low-fat (23); UK Stilton has no quantity limit (24); Swiss/Emmentaler with eyes (25: EU 27 22,900,000 kg).

**Note 26.** Eggs of wild birds may not be imported, except game-bird eggs for propagation under Interior Department rules and specimens for scientific collections.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 04 Dairy, Egg & Honey Tariff Updates — Canada Section 338, Section 301 & What Changed Since 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for dairy, egg and honey imports (HTS Chapter 04) since January 2025: the 50% Section 338 duties and whey ban on Canada, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, honey antidumping reviews and dairy quota licensing, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **All 272 Chapter 04 base rates are unchanged** — the dairy quotas, the over-quota rates and the egg and honey rates are the same as in January 2025.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** the 2026 Section 301 tariffs apply to goods of 60 economies — **10% in total for EU cheese and butter**, +12.5% for New Zealand, +10% for India, Argentina and the UK, +37.5% for Brazil. **Canada** got the sharpest change: a **50% Section 338 duty** on milk powders, whey and milk proteins and on honey from August 22, 2026, on most cheeses from September 15 — even with a USMCA claim — and an **import ban on Canadian whey from September 29, 2026**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 04 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the Canada Section 338 duties and dairy import ban, the Section 232 aluminum duty on Russian condensed milk, the Nicaragua Section 301 tariff that starts in 2027, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, the antidumping orders on honey, and USDA rules that changed what can enter. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). New Zealand has no FTA with the United States, but it holds large country quotas: 11,322,000 kg of "other" cheese and 8,200,000 kg of Cheddar, plus at least 5,678,117 liters of the cream quota. The 15% reciprocal IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from February 24 to July 23, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: New Zealand whey, milk proteins and butter — $477M of its $579M in 2025 — pay the base rate plus 12.5% of value: in-quota cheese at 10% becomes 22.5%, milk protein concentrate 0.37¢/kg + 12.5%, and manuka honey 1.9¢/kg + 12.5%.

inEffect.exemption: For EU goods whose base rate (or its ad valorem equivalent) is under 10%, the total is 10% (9903.05.39); goods with a higher base rate pay only the base rate. No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). No Chapter 04 line is on the EU exception list (9903.05.97). The 2019 aircraft-dispute duties on EU cheese, butter and yogurt (9903.89.xx) have been suspended since 2021. This replaced the 15% IEEPA reciprocal rate, which ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Low-rate EU goods move up to 10%: Pecorino Romano (Free), Roquefort (2.7%), in-quota butter (12.3¢/kg) and honey now pay 10% of value. Most EU cheese already paid more — 10% to 25% in quota, $1.055–$2.269/kg over quota — and pays the same as before.

inEffect.exemption: The 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.29) is lifted for goods entered free under USMCA (9903.05.93). The **Section 338 duties are not**: they apply even when USMCA or another preference is claimed (U.S. note 51(a)). 9903.03.13 (Proclamation 11047, dairy) covers 29 lines of milk powder, condensed milk, whey and milk proteins from August 22, 2026; 9903.03.14 covers honey (6 lines) from August 22 and 0406.90.99 from September 15; 9903.03.12 covers 24 cheese lines from September 15, 2026 (Proclamation 11064). Whey (0404.10, 9 lines) is banned from September 29, 2026 (Proclamation 11062). Eggs, butter, yogurt and most other lines are not on the lists. The 35% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying Canadian eggs, butter and yogurt still enter free. Canadian milk powder, milk protein, honey and most cheeses pay 50% of value on top of the base rate even with USMCA — $50,000 on a $100,000 load — and Canadian whey can no longer be imported (Canada shipped $68M of whey and milk proteins in 2025).

inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods entered free under USMCA pay no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). Mexican goods are excluded from every Chapter 04 quota (additional U.S. notes 5–25) — with a USMCA claim they enter free on any line, in or over quota. No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 exemption lists. The 25% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Mexican goods ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying Mexican milk powder ($102M in 2025), eggs, butter and honey pay $0. Goods that do not qualify pay the over-quota rate — Mexico has no in-quota access — plus 10% of value.

inEffect.exemption: No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). Raw honey from India is under an antidumping order (87 FR 35501, June 10, 2022): CBP collects a company-specific cash deposit set in Commerce's annual reviews (the latest final results were published June 18, 2026). The 25% reciprocal and the extra 25% IEEPA duty on India (from August 27, 2025) ended on February 7 and February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Indian honey — $180M in 2025, the largest honey source — pays 1.9¢/kg plus 10% of value plus the antidumping deposit on raw honey. Ghee and butter oil pay their base rate plus 10%.

inEffect.exemption: +25% under the Brazil action from July 22, 2026 (9903.05.01) and +12.5% under the forced-labor action from July 24, 2026 (9903.05.27). Only certified-organic honey (0409.00.00.05) is on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03), so it pays 12.5%; every other Chapter 04 line pays 37.5%. Raw honey from Brazil is also under an antidumping order (87 FR 35501). The 2025 IEEPA duties on Brazil (10% reciprocal plus 40%) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Brazilian honey ($104M in 2025) pays 1.9¢/kg plus 12.5% if certified organic, 37.5% if not, plus the antidumping deposit on raw honey. Brazilian eggs ($46M) pay 2.8¢/dozen plus 37.5% of value.

inEffect.exemption: No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). Argentina holds the largest Italian-type cheese quota (6,383,000 kg, note 21). Raw honey from Argentina is under an antidumping order (87 FR 35501); the latest final review results were published June 12, 2026 and preliminary results for 2024–2025 on September 14, 2026. The 10% reciprocal IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from February 24 to July 23, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Argentine honey ($139M in 2025) pays 1.9¢/kg plus 10% of value plus the antidumping deposit; in-quota Argentine Parmesan-type cheese pays 15% + 10% = 25%.

inEffect.exemption: Swiss goods with a base rate under 12.5% pay 12.5% in total (9903.05.74); a higher base rate applies alone. Edible insects (0410.10) are on Switzerland's exception list (U.S. note 52(j)(3), 9903.05.98) and pay only the base rate. Switzerland has its own cheese quotas (1,720,000 kg of "other" cheese, 1,850,000 kg of Swiss without eyes, 3,630,000 kg with eyes).
inEffect.whatItMeans: Swiss Emmentaler with eyes in quota (6.4%) now pays 12.5% in total; Gruyère in quota (10%) also 12.5%. Over-quota Swiss cheese ($1.386–$1.877/kg) already pays more than 12.5% and is unchanged.

inEffect.exemption: No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). UK goods have their own cheese quotas (2,213,374 kg of "other" cheese, 895,948 kg of Cheddar) and UK Stilton has no quantity limit (note 24). The 2019 aircraft-dispute duties on UK cheese have been suspended since 2021. The 10% reciprocal IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from February 24 to July 23, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: British cheese ($57M in 2025) and eggs ($23M) pay their base rate plus 10% of value: Stilton in original loaves at 12.8% becomes 22.8%, eggs 2.8¢/dozen + 10%.

inEffect.exemption: No Chapter 04 line is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). Raw honey from Vietnam is under an antidumping order with high rates (the 2022 Vietnam-wide rate was 60.03%); the latest final review results were published June 12, 2026. The 20% reciprocal IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from February 24 to July 23, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Vietnamese honey ($32M in 2025) pays 1.9¢/kg plus 12.5% of value plus the antidumping deposit, which for raw honey can be several times the tariff.

inEffect.exemption: Two Section 301 duties stack: +12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31, from July 24, 2026) and either +25% under List 3 (9903.88.03 — whey, butter, eggs, egg products, honey and insects, 28 lines) or +7.5% under List 4A (9903.88.15 — milk, milk powder, yogurt, cheese and the other 244 lines). Honey from China has been under an antidumping order since 2001, continued on October 3, 2023. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Chinese eggs ($10.5M in 2025) and honey pay their base rate plus 37.5% of value, and honey also the antidumping duty; Chinese cheese or milk powder pays the base rate plus 20%.

inEffect.exemption: Russian goods pay the Column 2 rates (normal trade relations were suspended in 2022) plus 12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.66). Sweetened condensed milk (0402.99.68, 0402.99.70, 0402.99.90) is on the Section 232 aluminum derivative list, and Russian goods on those lines pay the 200% aluminum duty (9903.85.68).
inEffect.whatItMeans: Russia supplies almost no Chapter 04 goods; any Russian dairy would pay Column 2 rates plus 12.5%, and condensed milk the 200% aluminum duty on top.

inEffect.country: Other Section 301 economies (48: Algeria, Angola, Australia, Bahamas, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Chile, …)
inEffect.now: +10% or 10% (in place of base) or +12.5% or 12.5% (in place of base)
inEffect.exemption: No Chapter 04 line is on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)). Edible insects (0410.10) are on the country exception lists of Cambodia, Ecuador, Indonesia, Jordan and Malaysia (U.S. note 52(j)) and pay only the base rate from those countries. Australia, Norway, Türkiye, Chile, Uruguay and Israel pay +12.5%; Costa Rica +12.5%. Countries outside the 60 economies pay no extra duty.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Turkish eggs ($29M in 2025) pay 2.8¢/dozen plus 12.5% of value; Chilean milk powder ($62M) pays its base rate (Free with a U.S.–Chile FTA claim) plus 12.5% — an FTA claim does not remove the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). Indonesian edible bird's nests pay 1.1% plus 10%.

changes.title: No Chapter 04 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 272 lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered. The dairy quota quantities in additional U.S. notes 5–25 are the same.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 duty: 10% from 2027, 15% from 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a phased duty on products of Nicaragua (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It does not apply to goods that originate under CAFTA-DR (U.S. note 29) — Nicaraguan cheese ($59M in 2025) entered with a CAFTA-DR claim stays outside it.

changes.title: Canadian whey banned from import
changes.detail: Proclamation 11062 excludes from importation the Canadian dairy products listed in its annex — in Chapter 04, all whey and modified whey of 0404.10 (9 lines) — for goods imported from 12:01 a.m. ET on September 29, 2026, because Canada kept its cheese quota rules. Goods imported before that date but not yet entered stay subject to the 50% duty. If the ban is struck down, the 50% applies instead.

changes.title: Proposed: shorter bird-flu waiting period for eggs and poultry products
changes.detail: APHIS proposed cutting the period in which birds and avian commodities — including table eggs under 9 CFR 94.6 — may not have been exposed to highly pathogenic avian influenza before export to the United States from 90 days to 28 days. Comments are due November 23, 2026; the 90-day rule still applies.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duty extended to most cheeses
changes.detail: Proclamation 11064 added cheese to the 9903.03.12 list from September 15, 2026 — 24 Chapter 04 lines of fresh, grated, processed, blue and other cheese, including Cheddar — and Proclamation 11065 added 0406.90.99 to the 9903.03.14 list. Like the other Section 338 duties, the 50% applies even with a USMCA claim (U.S. note 51(a)).

changes.title: Honey antidumping reviews: preliminary 2024–2025 rates for Argentina, Brazil and Vietnam
changes.detail: Commerce published preliminary results of the 2024–2025 administrative reviews of the raw-honey antidumping orders on Argentina, Brazil and Vietnam. Final results, normally due about 120 days later, will set new company-specific cash-deposit rates; until then the current deposits apply.

changes.title: 2027 dairy import licenses: $325 fee
changes.detail: USDA FAS set the fee for each 2027 dairy tariff-rate quota import license at $325 and moved some quantities from historical licenses (Appendix 1) to the lottery licenses (Appendix 2) for 2027.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties take effect: 50% on milk powders, whey, milk proteins and honey
changes.detail: Proclamation 11047 (dairy) put 50% on Canadian milk powder, condensed milk, whey and milk proteins (9903.03.13, 29 lines), and the motor-vehicle proclamation 11048 put honey on its list (9903.03.14, 6 lines). Set for August 19, the duties were suspended for three days (Proclamation 11056) and took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on August 22, 2026. They apply on top of the base rate and any Section 301 duty, including on USMCA-qualifying goods.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) — no Chapter 04 line is exempt. EU goods pay 10% in total and Japanese, Korean and Swiss goods 12.5% in total when the base rate is lower, so most EU cheese (base rate above 10%) pays nothing extra while EU butter in quota and honey move to 10%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). Edible insects are on six countries' exception lists.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. No Chapter 04 line was on its exemption list (9903.03.03).

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). Only certified-organic honey (0409.00.00.05) is on the exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) stacks on top, so Brazilian eggs and conventional honey pay 37.5%.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims still apply to Canadian and Mexican dairy, eggs and honey — though for Canada they no longer remove the Section 338 duties.

changes.title: Proposed changes to dairy quota import licensing
changes.detail: USDA FAS proposed rewriting the dairy tariff-rate quota licensing rule (7 CFR part 6): new license-transfer rules, stronger suspension and revocation, and an earlier surrender date so unused quantities can be reallocated sooner. Comments closed April 23, 2026 after a 15-day extension; no final rule yet.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026, including all Chapter 04 goods. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Additional 25% duty on products of India ended
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) that had applied since August 27, 2025 — on top of India's 25% reciprocal rate — to Indian honey, ghee and other dairy.

changes.title: Additional 25% duty on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% (9903.01.84) on products of India on top of the 25% reciprocal rate, so Indian honey paid 1.9¢/kg + 50% plus antidumping duties. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Russian condensed milk added to the 200% aluminum duty
changes.detail: Commerce added sweetened condensed milk (0402.99.68, 0402.99.70, 0402.99.90) to the Section 232 aluminum derivative list from August 18, 2025. The general derivative heading for these lines (9903.85.08) has since ended; Russian goods on them still pay 200% (9903.85.68).

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates, for example New Zealand +15%, India +25%, Vietnam +20%, and for EU goods 15% in total including the base rate (or the base rate if higher). No Chapter 04 line was on the reciprocal exemption list. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 40% IEEPA duty on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 (signed July 30, 2025) added 40% on goods of Brazil from August 6, 2025, on top of the 10% reciprocal duty — 50% in all on Brazilian honey and eggs. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). USMCA-qualifying dairy, eggs and honey stayed exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025 on all Chapter 04 goods except those of Canada and Mexico; country rates followed on August 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

effectiveDuty.note: Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet. Much of the trade enters in quota or free under USMCA and FTA claims; the over-quota dairy rates, the honey antidumping duties and the 2025–2026 extra duties are what raise the bill.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 04 goods fell from **$4.49B in 2024 to $4.06B in 2025** (−9.7%), after growing every year since 2020 ($2.70B). The drop is almost all **butter and cheese from Europe**: butter (0405) fell from $826M to $494M (−40%) and cheese (0406) from $2.00B to $1.70B (−15%). Ireland, the largest butter supplier, halved from $641M to $318M, and Italy fell from $536M to $398M. 2025 was the year EU goods paid the 10% reciprocal duty from April and 15% in total from August 7.

Two products went the other way. **Egg imports more than doubled**, from $92M to $221M, and fresh table eggs (0407.21) from $7M to $122M, as avian influenza cut the U.S. laying flock — Brazil, Canada, Mexico, Türkiye and the UK filled the gap. **Honey** rose 6% to $691M; India ($180M), Argentina ($139M) and Brazil ($104M, +65% for all Brazilian Chapter 04 goods) remain the main sources despite the antidumping duties on raw honey.

New Zealand stayed the largest supplier ($579M), mostly whey, milk proteins and butter used by U.S. food and nutrition makers. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so the 2026 Section 301 and Canada Section 338 duties are not yet visible in these figures.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on dairy, eggs and honey depends on **what it is, where it comes from and whether it enters in quota**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator.

**EU goods pay at least 10% in total** — most EU cheese already paid more and is unchanged, while in-quota butter and honey move up to 10%. New Zealand, Vietnam and Brazil pay +12.5% (Brazil +37.5% on all but organic honey), India, Argentina and the UK +10%, Switzerland 12.5% in total. **Canada** pays +10% unless USMCA applies, and **50% on milk powders, milk proteins, honey and most cheeses even with USMCA**; its whey is banned. USMCA-qualifying Mexican goods enter free on every line.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-12, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Preferences: USMCA (S, S+) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side. No other FTA is applied — none of the listed countries other than Canada and Mexico has an FTA with the United States. GSP (A, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and is not applied. An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)), and for Canada it does not remove the Section 338 duty (U.S. note 51(a)).
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

In quota vs. over quota: most dairy groups mix in-quota lines (low rates, usually needing a USDA import license and the country's quota to be open) and "Other" over-quota lines with high per-kilogram rates. Which applies depends on the license and the quota on the entry date; select a cell to see the lines.
Antidumping duties on raw honey from Argentina, Brazil, India and Vietnam and on honey from China are company-specific cash deposits set by Commerce and are not included in the totals.

Special agricultural safeguard duties (Chapter 99, subchapter IV), footnoted on many over-quota dairy lines, can add to the over-quota rate when the entered price is below the trigger price; they are not included.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.

The rate is not the only gate: fluid milk and cream need an FDA import milk permit, eggs and egg products need USDA approval, and APHIS rules for foot-and-mouth disease and avian influenza can bar dairy or eggs from a region regardless of the tariff.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 04: Dairy Produce; Birds' Eggs; Natural Honey; Edible Products of Animal Origin, Not Elsewhere Specified or Included — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Dairy, Cheese, Eggs & Honey into the U.S.: Licenses, FDA & USDA Rules, Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 04) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The documents and rules for each HTS Chapter 04 line — USDA dairy import licenses, the FDA import milk permit, prior notice and FSVP, APHIS disease rules, AMS shell-egg and FSIS egg-product rules, honey antidumping duties — and the legal ways to pay less: quota licenses, USMCA and FTA claims, Chapter 98, drawback.
keywords: importing milk into the us fda permit

tariffEngineering.intro:
For dairy the first question is **which line you can enter under**. Most dairy products have an in-quota line with a low rate that needs a **USDA dairy import license** (or a general note 15 purpose), and an over-quota line at $0.31 to $2.27 per kilogram. Fluid milk and cream also need an **FDA import milk permit**; all of it needs FDA prior notice and a foreign supplier verification program, and APHIS disease rules decide which countries can ship. Eggs follow USDA rules — AMS for shell eggs, FSIS for egg products — and honey is an ordinary FDA food but carries **antidumping duties** from five countries.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: **get a dairy license**, **claim USMCA or an FTA**, or use a **Chapter 98** provision when the purpose fits. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Enter dairy in quota with a USDA import license
levers.saves: The difference between the over-quota and in-quota rate — on 10 t of cheese at $8/kg, $1.509/kg ($15,090) vs. 10% ($8,000)
levers.appliesTo: Cheese, butter, milk powder, dried whey, cream and other lines "described in additional U.S. note 5–25 to this chapter" (vs. the "Other" over-quota lines)
levers.document: A dairy import license from USDA FAS for the quota year and the article and country (historical, lottery or designated license), applied for under 7 CFR part 6; the license number goes on the entry. The 2027 fee is $325 per license. Goods described in general note 15 (such as U.S. government or small personal-use and sample imports) can use the general note 15 lines without a license.
levers.caveat: Licenses are issued for a calendar year and a supplying country; unused quantities can be surrendered and reallocated. Mexican goods cannot enter under the quota lines. Canadian aged raw-milk cheddar under note 18(c) needs no license but must be certified by the Canadian government.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on dairy, eggs and honey from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate (up to $2.27/kg over quota) and the 10% Section 301 duty — but not the Canada Section 338 duty
levers.appliesTo: All 272 lines for qualifying Mexican goods (in or over quota); Canadian goods inside Canada's USMCA quantities (9823.xx) or on lines whose Special column lists S
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: For Canada the 50% Section 338 duty applies even with a USMCA claim on 60 lines (U.S. note 51(a)), and whey cannot be imported at all from September 29, 2026. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim a free trade agreement (Chile, CAFTA-DR, Peru, Colombia, Korea, Australia and others)
levers.saves: The base rate, including over-quota rates on the lines where the agreement gives duty-free access; the Section 301 duty stays
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose Special column lists the agreement (AU, BH, CL, CO, IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P, PA, PE, SG); several agreements have their own dairy quotas in Chapter 98 and 99 (e.g. 9822.04.xx for Australia, 9918.04.xx for Colombia, 9919.04.xx for Panama)
levers.document: A claim on the entry with the agreement's certification or origin information — for example Chile (19 CFR 10.410), CAFTA-DR (19 CFR 10.583) or Australia (19 CFR 10.703).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim does not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)): Chilean milk powder still pays 12.5%. Over-quota access under an FTA is usually its own quantity, first come, first served.

levers.title: Classify cheese by type — some cheeses have no quota
levers.saves: The whole over-quota rate: sheep's-milk Pecorino in original loaves is Free, other sheep's-milk cheese 9.6% and Roquefort 2.7%–4.5%, with no license needed
levers.appliesTo: Cheese of 0406 that is outside the quotas: cheese not containing cow's milk, soft-ripened cow's milk cheese (additional U.S. note 3), and the named cheeses with their own lines
levers.document: Product specifications showing the milk type, fat and moisture content and ripening (for soft-ripened cheese the note 3 criteria).
levers.caveat: The exclusion depends on the facts: a cheese with any cow's milk, or with mold throughout the interior, falls back into a quota line. A binding ruling settles it.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 4, additional U.S. notes 3 and 16

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the facts fit
levers.saves: The base rate and the Section 301 and Section 338 duties: the provision below is Free
levers.appliesTo: U.S. dairy, eggs or honey that were exported and come back without being processed abroad (for example a rejected export shipment)
levers.document: Proof that the goods are U.S. products returned unchanged, and the FDA or USDA clearance that applies to the returned product.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties and the Canada Section 338 duties do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate, except 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 entries (U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(a)).

provisions.text: Products of the United States returned after export without being advanced in value or improved in condition abroad

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51(a) and 52(a)

levers.title: Claim drawback when imported dairy or honey is exported again
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on goods that are exported or used to make exported products
levers.appliesTo: Any line, when the imported product (or substitutable product under the same 8-digit subheading) is exported — for example milk powder or whey used in exported food
levers.document: A drawback claim with import and export records linking the two.
levers.caveat: Antidumping duties are not refundable as drawback, and not every extra duty is eligible; confirm with CBP which duties on your entry can be refunded before pricing on it.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (cheese type, whey vs. milk protein, butter vs. butter oil, retail-packed vs. raw honey) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate or whether an antidumping order applies
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product and the intended entry.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own. Whether honey is inside an antidumping order is decided by Commerce, not CBP.

rules.title: Prior notice before arrival and a foreign supplier verification program for all food in the chapter
Federal Import Milk Act: a permit, farm and plant inspections and bacteria limits for fluid milk and cream
Milk and milk products in final package form for consumers must be pasteurized; raw-milk cheese must meet the aging rules of its standard
Dairy import license for in-quota entry of quota cheese, butter, milk powder, dried whey and other licensed articles
Foot-and-mouth disease: milk and milk products from affected regions only under processing or certification conditions
Avian influenza and Newcastle disease: conditions on eggs from affected regions; hatching eggs need an APHIS import permit and quarantine
Shell eggs: restricted eggs only within U.S. Consumer Grade B tolerances; importer must meet AMS shell-egg import rules
Shell eggs for retail must be kept at 45°F or below and carry the safe-handling statement; producers follow the egg safety rule
Egg products only from countries FSIS has found eligible, with a foreign inspection certificate and FSIS import inspection
Eggs of wild birds may not be imported, except game-bird eggs for propagation and scientific specimens
Antidumping cash deposits on raw honey from Argentina, Brazil, India and Vietnam and on honey from China
Canada Section 338: report the 9903.03.12–9903.03.14 heading on Canadian lines listed in U.S. note 51; Canadian whey is excluded from entry

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 51

groups.label: Milk and cream, not concentrated or sweetened
groups.note: Fluid milk and cream need an FDA import milk permit for each shipper; the over-6%-fat lines are under quota.

groups.label: Milk and cream, concentrated or sweetened (milk powder, condensed milk)
groups.note: In-quota milk powder needs a USDA license; Canadian product pays the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Yogurt, buttermilk, sour cream, kefir
groups.note: Yogurt has one rate (17%); dried fermented milk and sour cream follow the milk powder and cream quotas.

groups.label: Whey and milk protein products
groups.note: Dried whey is under quota; whey protein and milk protein concentrates are not. Canadian whey (0404.10) is banned from September 29, 2026.

groups.label: Butter, butter oil, ghee and dairy spreads
groups.note: The butter quota is only 6,977 t a year and needs a USDA license; the over-quota rate is $1.541/kg.

groups.label: Cheese and curd
groups.note: Most cheeses need a USDA license to use the in-quota line; cheeses without cow's milk and soft-ripened cheese are outside the quotas. Raw-milk cheese must meet the aging rules of its FDA standard.

groups.label: Birds' eggs, in shell
groups.note: Bird-flu restrictions can close a region at short notice; hatching eggs need an APHIS permit.

groups.label: Eggs not in shell and egg yolks
groups.note: Egg products are FSIS-regulated: the exporting country must be eligible and each lot certified.

groups.label: Natural honey
groups.note: Check whether the honey is inside an antidumping order (raw honey from AR, BR, IN, VN; honey from CN) before pricing.

groups.label: Insects and other edible animal products
groups.note: Edible insects and bird's nests are FDA-regulated foods; bird's nests may also face APHIS avian rules.

seo.title: Dairy, Cheese, Egg & Honey Tariffs FAQ: EU Cheese, Canadian Dairy, Honey, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 04) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about dairy, cheese, egg and honey tariffs: the tariff on EU and Italian cheese, Canadian dairy and the whey ban, Irish butter, honey from India and Argentina, egg imports, HS codes for cheese, honey and whey, and how to import cheese into the U.S.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing dairy, cheese, eggs and honey into the U.S. — tariffs by country, the dairy quotas, the Canada duties, honey antidumping duties, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Most dairy has two rates: a low in-quota rate that usually needs a USDA import license, and a high over-quota rate — $1.055 to $2.269/kg for cheese, $1.541/kg for butter. Eggs (2.8¢/dozen) and honey (1.9¢/kg) have one small rate.

Since July 24, 2026 goods of 60 economies pay a Section 301 duty: EU goods 10% in total (most EU cheese already paid more and is unchanged), New Zealand and Vietnam +12.5%, India, Argentina and the UK +10%, Brazil +37.5%. USMCA-qualifying Mexican goods enter free.

Canadian milk powder, milk protein, honey and most cheese pay an extra 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA, and Canadian whey is banned from September 29, 2026. Raw honey from Argentina, Brazil, India, Vietnam and China also pays antidumping duties.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on imported cheese right now?
faqs.answer: It depends on the cheese and whether it enters in quota. Most cheeses have an in-quota rate of about 10% to 25% (using a USDA import license) and an over-quota rate of $1.055 to $2.269 per kg. Some cheeses are outside the quotas and need no license: sheep's-milk Pecorino in original loaves is Free, Roquefort 2.7%–4.5%, and soft-ripened cheese such as Brie and cheese without cow's milk are not counted against the quotas. On top, goods of the 60 Section 301 economies pay an extra duty since July 24, 2026 — EU cheese 10% in total, which adds nothing to most EU cheese because its rate is already higher.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on cheese from Italy, France and the EU?
faqs.answer: EU cheese pays its base rate, or 10% in total if the base rate is lower (Section 301, 9903.05.39, since July 24, 2026). Parmigiano Reggiano in quota pays 15% and over quota $2.146/kg; Gouda 15% in quota or $1.803/kg; Pecorino Romano moves from Free to 10%. From August 7, 2025 to February 24, 2026 EU goods paid 15% in total under the IEEPA reciprocal tariff, which has ended. Italy ($391M) and France ($265M) were the largest cheese suppliers in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a U.S. tariff on Canadian dairy and cheese?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 338, Canadian milk powder, condensed milk, whey and milk proteins pay an extra 50% since August 22, 2026 (9903.03.13), most cheeses since September 15, 2026 (9903.03.12), and honey since August 22 (9903.03.14) — even with a USMCA claim. Canadian whey (0404.10) is banned from import from September 29, 2026 (Proclamation 11062). Non-USMCA goods also pay the 10% Section 301 duty. USMCA-qualifying Canadian eggs, butter and yogurt still enter free.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Irish (Kerrygold-type) butter?
faqs.answer: Most imported butter pays the over-quota rate of $1.541 per kg (0405.10.20), about 22% on butter worth $7/kg, because the butter quota is only 6,977 t a year for all countries and needs a USDA license. In quota the rate is 12.3¢/kg, which the EU Section 301 rule lifts to 10% of value. Ireland shipped $209M of butter to the U.S. in 2025, down from about twice that in 2024.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on imported honey?
faqs.answer: The base rate is 1.9¢ per kg, plus the Section 301 duty of the country of origin: +10% for India and Argentina, +12.5% for New Zealand and Vietnam, +37.5% for Brazil (+12.5% for certified-organic Brazilian honey) and +37.5% for China. Canadian honey pays an extra 50%. Raw honey from Argentina, Brazil, India and Vietnam and honey from China also pay antidumping cash deposits set by Commerce.

faqs.question: Which countries have antidumping duties on honey?
faqs.answer: Raw honey from Argentina, Brazil, India and Vietnam has been under antidumping orders since June 10, 2022 (87 FR 35501); honey packed for retail sale in containers of 5 lb or less is excluded. Honey from China has been under an order since 2001, continued on October 3, 2023. Rates are company-specific and reset in yearly reviews: the 2022 "all others" rates were 16.92% (Argentina), 7.89% (Brazil), 5.87% (India) and 60.03% (Vietnam-wide).

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on imported eggs, and where does the U.S. import eggs from?
searchedAs: where does the us import eggs from
faqs.answer: Eggs in shell pay 2.8¢ per dozen, plus the Section 301 duty of the country — +37.5% for Brazil, +12.5% for Türkiye, +10% for the UK; USMCA-qualifying eggs from Canada and Mexico are free. Egg imports rose from $92M in 2024 to $221M in 2025 after avian influenza cut U.S. supply; Brazil ($46M), Canada ($45M), Mexico ($36M), Türkiye ($29M) and the UK ($23M) were the main sources. Shipments need USDA approval under the APHIS bird-flu rules.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on dairy from New Zealand?
faqs.answer: New Zealand goods pay their base rate plus 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.57). Milk protein concentrate pays 0.37¢/kg + 12.5%, whey protein concentrate 8.5% + 12.5% = 21%, in-quota cheese 10% + 12.5% = 22.5%. New Zealand was the largest Chapter 04 supplier in 2025 ($579M), mostly whey, milk proteins and butter.

faqs.question: How do the U.S. dairy import quotas work?
faqs.answer: They are tariff-rate quotas, not bans. Each year a set quantity of cheese, butter, milk powder, cream and other dairy enters at a low in-quota rate, mostly with a USDA FAS import license (7 CFR part 6) tied to a supplying country; anything over that pays the over-quota rate. Quantities are in additional U.S. notes 5–25 to Chapter 4 — for example 6,977 t of butter and 25,633 t of "other" cheese for the EU. Mexico is excluded from the quotas and enters free under USMCA.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for cheese?
faqs.answer: Cheese is heading 0406: fresh cheese such as mozzarella and ricotta 0406.10, grated or powdered 0406.20, processed 0406.30, blue-veined 0406.40 and all other cheese 0406.90 — Cheddar 0406.90.06–.12, Gouda and Edam 0406.90.14–.18, Parmesan and Romano 0406.90.39–.43, Swiss with eyes 0406.90.44–.48. The U.S. lines then split by in-quota and over-quota entry. 0406.90 was the largest product in the chapter in 2025 ($1.47B).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for honey?
faqs.answer: Natural honey is 0409.00.00, split for U.S. statistics into certified organic (.05), comb honey and honey packed for retail sale (.10), and bulk honey by color: white (.35), extra light amber (.45), light amber (.56) and amber or darker (.65). All pay 1.9¢/kg. Artificial honey and honey blends are in 1702 or 2106.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for whey protein and milk powder?
searchedAs: hs code for skim milk powder
hs code for milk protein concentrate
faqs.answer: Whey and whey protein concentrate are 0404.10 (whey protein concentrate 0404.10.05 at 8.5%); milk protein concentrate is 0404.90.10 (0.37¢/kg). Whey protein isolate over 80% protein is an albumin in 3502. Skim milk powder is 0402.10 and whole milk powder 0402.21, with in-quota and over-quota lines.

faqs.question: Can you import cheese and dairy into the U.S., and what do you need?
searchedAs: how to import cheese into the us
importing dairy products into the us
faqs.answer: Yes. Every shipment needs FDA prior notice (21 CFR 1.281) and the importer a foreign supplier verification program (21 CFR 1.502). Quota cheese, butter and milk powder need a USDA dairy import license to use the low in-quota rate (7 CFR part 6). Fluid milk and cream need an FDA import milk permit (21 CFR part 1210), and APHIS restricts milk products from foot-and-mouth-disease regions (9 CFR 94.16). Raw-milk cheese must meet the aging rules of its FDA standard.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import its dairy, cheese and honey from?
faqs.answer: $4.06B of Chapter 04 goods in 2025, down 9.7% from 2024: New Zealand $579M, Italy $398M, France $375M, Canada $337M, Ireland $318M, Mexico $269M, India $217M, Brazil $161M, Argentina $156M and the Netherlands $148M. Cheese was $1.70B (Italy and France lead), honey $691M (India, Argentina, Brazil) and butter $494M (Ireland, New Zealand).
